title: When {recipient} says no
notes: DRAFT for content-owner review. Same for everyone: no setup question and no variants. Every by-variant block has one 'default' entry and every *VariantMap is empty.
Placeholders as in quiz.json: {recipient}, {Recipient}, {possessive}, {Possessive}, {object}. The subject is always {recipient}, never {pronoun}.
Default example is a refused shower and getting dressed: neutral everyday moments. Heavier refusals are not covered here.
Same three steps as lessons 1 to 3; here the third step is a small choice instead of 'help look'.
Every screen shows the line from common.notMedicalAdvice in the footer.

steps.label: Reassure
steps.example: That's okay. I'm here, and there's no rush.

steps.label: Offer a small choice
steps.example: Would you like to wash up now, or after your tea?

default.setup: It's morning. You say it's time for a shower. {Recipient} crosses {possessive} arms and says:
default.line: I don't want a shower. I don't need one.

screens.question: What would you say?

default.text: You have to. You haven't had one in ages.
default.feedback: Almost everyone says this. You care about {possessive} comfort. But "you have to" tends to make the no firmer.

default.text: Just get in. It'll only take five minutes.
default.feedback: It's hopeful and quick. But pushing can feel like being rushed, and a rushed person often digs in.

default.text: All right, we'll skip it today.
default.feedback: Kind, and it ends the standoff. It gives no way forward, though, so the same moment comes back tomorrow.

default.text: You'd rather not right now. That's okay, there's no rush. Would you like to wash up now, or after your tea?
default.feedback: This names the feeling, reassures {object}, and offers a small choice. {Recipient} still has a say, and you get a way forward.

screens.afterChoice: You can try another answer to compare.

screens.title: A no often has a feeling behind it.
screens.body: Help with private things, like washing or getting dressed, can feel rushed or scary. A no can mean "I'm cold", "I'm tired", or "I want a say." {Recipient} isn't trying to make your day hard. Often, it's the feeling of losing control that says no.

options.label: Rushed, or not in control
options.response: Often, yes. Having a say matters, especially in private moments.

options.label: Wanting to make my day hard
options.response: It can feel that way when you're tired. Good instinct to take it seriously. Usually it's a feeling about the moment, not about you.

options.label: Not caring about being clean
options.response: It can look like that. Often it's the experience of being helped that is hard, not the cleaning.

screens.title: Don't push. Offer a small choice.
screens.body: A choice gives back a bit of control. Use the three steps: notice the feeling, reassure {object} that there's no rush, and offer two easy options, both fine with you. Avoid yes-or-no questions, since "no" is an easy answer.

miniTask.question: Which reply follows all three steps?

options.label: Come on, it's shower time. Do you want to do it or not?
options.response: Understandable. But a yes-or-no question invites another no, and it skips the feeling.

options.label: You'd rather not right now. That's okay, I'm here. Shower now, or after breakfast?
options.response: Yes: feeling, reassurance, and a small choice.

screens.title: Keep the choice small, and try again later.
screens.body: Two options is plenty: the blue top or the green one, now or after tea. If the answer is still no, let it rest. Try again in a little while, after a snack or a quiet moment. A no at nine can be a yes at eleven.

screens.title: Hearing no again and again is tiring. Pause first.
screens.body: It's normal to feel worn down, even when you know the no isn't about you. A small pause before you answer helps you stay kind.

miniTask.question: Pick your pause for next time:

options.label: One slow breath before I answer
Tell myself: this is a feeling, not a fight
Step away and try again in a little while, if it's safe

fallbackScenarios.setup: Morning. It's time to get dressed. {Recipient} says:
fallbackScenarios.line: I'm not getting dressed. I don't want to.

answers.text: You can't stay in your nightclothes all day.
answers.feedback: It's true, and you're trying to get things moving. But it can sound like an order, and the no gets firmer.

answers.text: You don't feel like it yet. That's okay, no rush. Would you like the blue top or the green one?
answers.feedback: Feeling, reassurance, and a small choice.
Calm and gentle. Adding a kind word and a small choice would give a way forward.

fallbackScenarios.setup: Later, you mention the shower. {Recipient} says:
fallbackScenarios.line: I don't need your help. Leave me alone.

answers.text: I'm only trying to help! Why are you so difficult?
answers.feedback: Being pushed away hurts. Stepping back from the sting, even silently, helps you stay calm.

answers.text: I'm only trying to help, but fine.
answers.feedback: It ends the tension. A word about how {recipient} feels would make it warmer.

answers.text: You'd like to do this on your own. I'm nearby if you need me. Shall I set out a towel, or wait outside?
answers.feedback: You named the wish for independence, stayed close, and gave a small choice.

fallbackScenarios.setup: Afternoon. You hold out {possessive} jacket for a short walk. {Recipient} says:

answers.text: Come on, some fresh air will do you good.
answers.feedback: Well meant. But it's a push, and a firm no often gets firmer.

answers.text: Staying put feels better right now. That's okay. Shall we go out for a few minutes now, or sit by the window and have tea first?
answers.feedback: You noticed the feeling, took the pressure off, and offered a choice.
Kind and calm. A small choice for later would keep the door open.

default.question: Did {recipient} say no to help since yesterday?

options.label: Not yet
options.response: Your plan is ready for when it does.

options.label: It helped
options.response: That's real progress. A small choice gives back a sense of control.

options.label: Partly
options.response: That's normal at first. Keep the same calm words for a few days. Familiar words help.

options.label: It didn't help
options.response: That happens. Here are a few more ways to try.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Try again later
followUpsDidntHelp.text: A no in the morning can become a yes after a snack or a rest. Let it go for now and come back in a little while.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Keep the same order
followUpsDidntHelp.text: Doing things at the same time and in the same order each day makes them feel less like a request.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Let {recipient} do a part
followUpsDidntHelp.text: Hand over the washcloth or the brush. Doing one small part feels like having a say.

doctorNote.text: If {recipient} suddenly says no to things that used to be fine, or seems uncomfortable when helped, mention it at the next doctor visit.
